title: What Are Your Fundamental Rights?
summary: The rights the Constitution gives every person in India, and what they really mean in daily life.

body.text: The Constitution gives every person in India some basic rights. No one can just take them away. Not the police, not your boss, not the government. These rights are called Fundamental Rights.

items: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18): the law must treat everyone the same.
Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22): you can speak, move around, and you get protection when you are arrested.
Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24): no one can force you to work, and children cannot be made to work.
Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28): you are free to follow your religion.
Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30): your culture and your right to study are protected.
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32): if someone breaks your right, you can go to court.

body.text: Article 21 is about the right to life and personal freedom. The Supreme Court has said it also covers dignity (respect), privacy (your private life), health, and a clean environment.
⚖️ How these rights help you every day

If a shop refuses to serve you just because of your religion or caste, that is a problem of equality. If the police hold you and do not tell you why, that is a problem of freedom. If your employer does not pay your salary for many months, courts have linked fair pay to the right to life.
⚖️ Rights come with duties and limits

items: Freedom of speech does not protect threats, hate speech, or defamation (saying false things to spoil someone's name).
Most rights have reasonable limits for the good of everyone.
Every right comes with a duty: respect other people's rights and follow the law.
Your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) gives free legal help to people who qualify.
You can call the NALSA helpline 15100 for guidance.
If a government action breaks a Fundamental Right, Article 32 lets you go straight to the Supreme Court, or Article 226 lets you go to a High Court.
Free legal aid is under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

body.text: Rights have limits. Freedom of speech does not protect threats, hate speech, or defamation (saying false things to spoil someone's name).
If you are not sure, ask for the reason in writing. Keep a copy of everything.

items: Article 14: equality before the law.
Article 15: no discrimination.
Article 16: equal opportunity in public employment.
Article 19: freedoms (speech, assembly, movement and more).
Article 21: life and personal liberty.
Article 21A: free education for ages 6 to 14.
Article 22: safeguards on arrest.
Article 23: no trafficking or forced labour.
Article 24: no child labour under 14.
Articles 25-28: religion.
Articles 29-30: cultural and educational rights.
Article 32: move the Supreme Court.
Article 226: move a High Court.
Some rights are for every person in India, citizen or not.
A few rights (Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29) are only for citizens.
Article 51A lists the Fundamental Duties of citizens.

practicalSteps: Write down what happened. Note the date, place, and names.
Keep copies of all documents, messages, and receipts.
If any right is limited, ask for the reason in writing.
For free help, contact your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or call the NALSA helpline 15100.
exceptions: Some rights can be limited during a declared emergency (Articles 352-360). But Articles 20 and 21 can never be stopped.
Reasonable limits are allowed for the good of everyone, for example to keep public order or decency.

faqs.q: Can a private company break my Fundamental Rights?
faqs.a: Fundamental Rights are mostly against the State (the government). Against private people or companies, you usually use ordinary laws like contract law, labour law, and consumer law. A few rights, like Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24, do apply to private persons too.

faqs.q: Is free legal aid really free?
faqs.a: Yes, for people who qualify by income and category. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, every district has a Legal Services Authority.

misconceptions.myth: Fundamental Rights are only for citizens.
misconceptions.fact: Most of them apply to every person in India. A few, like Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29, apply only to citizens.
